 Iowa's Blue Wave Sent a Powerful Message About Democracy
 Iowa's election results reflected voter frustration with negativity and division.
 Opinion
 An Iowa voter counted 26 political mailers in the Hinson-Turek Senate race. Only two addressed issues. Here’s why a peaceful, accepted Election Day matters.
 By Amy Lockard Nov 18, 2026 Amy Lockard 
 Amy Lockard has a Master’s Degree in English Literature from the University of Northern Iowa (1994)
 and has continued classes at the Iowa Writers' Workshop. She has published several short stories, and poetry. She regularly contributes to regional newspapers and periodicals, combining her background in literature with commentary on modern politics and social issues. Currently she is working on the second of a four book fictional series based on Jane Austen’s “Pride and Prejudice." 
 See More Writings by author 
 Although Iowa is about as far from an ocean as is possible, the state was hit by a tsunami last week, or what political pundits are calling the “blue wave.” In Iowa's most hotly contested election in history, the outcome helped shift the balance of power in both the U.S. House and Senate. 
 Like Americans from every highly competitive race in these critical “tipping point” states, Iowans were besieged with political texts and surveys beginning months before the November election. Incessant negative radio and television political advertisements played day and night threateningly, like a far-too-early marathon of Jamie Lee Curtis’s “Halloween” movies.
 And the mail! Every day, Iowans’ mailboxes were stuffed with political flyers, most of them about our Senate race. Three-quarters supported Republican candidate Ashley Hinson, a congresswoman from the second district who represented Iowa in Washington, DC. PACs played a big role in the Republican race; among them were the SLF PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund—the single largest outside spender in Iowa’s Senate Race—and some “from the President” himself. Oh, the horrors these relentless mailings foretold: “A real ghost in Iowa’s cornfields,” “our daughters are in grave danger,” “anarchy,” “defunding all law enforcement,” “you will be joining Communist Vladimir Lenin.”
 Two days before election day, President Trump visited Iowa and said, “A vote for any Democrat anywhere in the country is a vote to put a deranged group of extremists into power.” 
 The Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate from Iowa was Josh Turek, a former state legislator from Iowa House District 20, who also received his share of mailings. Most came from the Iowa Democratic Party, as Turek had stated he does not take corporate PAC money. 
 By no means was the deluge of negative advertising limited just to the Republican Party or to the Senatorial race. Every race in the state, and likely in the country, had its own brand of “fright night” ads splayed across different media.
 But the sensationalism and the threats and the negative innuendos did not work. 
 Instead, we, the people, said with our votes: We are tired of negativity, of viperous and erratic disagreement. We do not condone a war not officially declared, a Congress that acts as if it is under hypnosis, a president who cares more about building a legacy than building a nation, erratic tariffs, threats or cruelty to any people, the bullying of our allies, or any form of unnecessary economic hardship upon our citizens.
 We said as well: PACS and billionaires (and in one notable case, a trillionaire) do not control us, and they will not control our elections. We do not condone bribery (President Trump’s erroneous promise of $5,000 to every voter if the Legislature remained Republican-controlled) 
 In other words: Americans’ votes are not for sale. 
 So, “Happy Election Day!” Not because of the “blue wave,” but because our elections matter so much to our democracy, and every individual citizen’s vote matters, too. 
 Blue as that wave may have looked, it was NOT just blue. It held our flag’s colors, a wave rolling across oceans to crash on the shores of every country and showing the world how democracy is done.
 That is not to say we are done. Or that we are ever done, balancing and rebalancing. Which is exactly what our Constitution anticipated and why it implemented checks and balances. And that is exactly what our election was really all about.
 Some insist on seeing it as a referendum on MAGA , or President Trump. Yes, but there’s a much deeper message behind the votes, and it's more profound. 
 We have “spoken” in this election as a free nation. This meaning matters more and is more intrinsic than any political party’s victory. 
 In essence, all of our citizens “won,” regardless of the “color” of their politics. We all won by holding a free election, even when there were palpable threats to do otherwise. We won by telling those who represent us what the American people want. And what we do not want.
 We won by telling the candidates we’ll send to Washington, DC, and to our state governments that we expect them to work for us, cooperate on our behalf, and undertake the serious task of finding real, workable solutions. 
 We won by insisting those we elect to govern do their jobs. 
 Although far from the “sea to shining sea” here in Iowa, we are part of the crest of this wave. We ALL are, as citizens of this diverse, vast, and magnificent country.
 And we are also all bearers of a bold, inspiring message.
 The message is this: “America works!” 
 Amy Lockard is an Iowa resident who regularly contributes to regional newspapers and periodicals. She is working on the second of a four-book fictional series based on Jane Austen’s “Pride and Prejudice."

 A Big Tent Revival: Faith and Pluralism in the 2026 Midterms
 F. Willis Johnson 
 Nov 17, 2026 
 The morning after the Democratic electoral tsunami, the map looked different. Democrats reclaimed both chambers of Congress, won in states long treated as Republican strongholds, and strengthened their hold in Pennsylvania. James Talarico prevailed in Texas. Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, won in Kansas. Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan made him the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. Wes Moore and Josh Shapiro won reelection as governors. The results rebuked President Donald Trump and his party. They also invited voters to ask what kind of public life they want next. 
 The familiar phrase “big tent” describes a coalition broad enough to gather people with different histories, beliefs, and priorities. But this election suggests something more active: a Big Tent Revival. A revival is not just a gathering. It is a call to renewal, a test of whether shared conviction can become changed practice. The election has opened that question. The answer will come in the work of governing.
 Consider the candidates whose victories helped give the night its breadth. Moore has spoken of faith as a source of service and moral responsibility. Talarico, a Christian and seminary student, has argued that faith can shape public commitments without giving government license to privilege one religion. Hamilton, a pastor before entering the Senate, said he would defend people's rights whether they have faith or not. These are distinct expressions of religious conviction, but each points toward a public ethic concerned with the lives and dignity of others. 
 Shapiro’s Jewish faith brings another moral tradition into view. His public language has drawn on tikkun olam, the Jewish call to repair the world. El-Sayed’s election carries a different significance: a Muslim American will enter a Senate where no Muslim has served before. His victory does not make him a proxy for every Muslim, just as Shapiro cannot be asked to represent every Jewish American. It does challenge the persistent assumption that some faith communities are guests in American civic life rather than participants. 
 The coalition’s importance lies in this combination of difference and common purpose. Voters did not have to share a theology to support candidates who spoke to everyday concerns: economic security, health care, education, safety, and the dignity of work. Nor did the candidates need to hide the sources of their moral commitments. The task was to translate conviction into a public program that could serve people beyond a single congregation, community, or party.
 That distinction matters. Faith in the public square can widen our concern for one another; it can also be wielded to divide the worthy from the unworthy. Religious language is not proof of good leadership. A politician’s claim to faith deserves the same scrutiny as any other claim: Does it lead to service? Does it help carry the burdens people face? Does it honor the equal dignity of neighbors who worship differently—or not at all?
 In my socio-theological commentary, I have returned to a basic question: Does our faith enlarge the circle of care, or narrow it? The answer cannot rest on how often a leader invokes God. It must be visible in choices—in whose needs count, whose voices are heard, and whether public power is used to repair harm or reinforce exclusion. A faith-informed politics is credible when it makes room for the vulnerable and holds the powerful accountable.
 That is why “revival” is the right word only if it comes with responsibility. Election-night speeches can promise a new chapter; governing writes the sentences. The new majority will have to show that it heard the people who made this result possible. That means translating empathy into policy, and policy into tangible improvements in people’s lives. It also means governing with enough humility to recognize that a broad coalition contains real disagreements, not just convenient campaign imagery.
 The tent will not hold because its members agree about everything. It will hold if they can work together without requiring anyone to surrender a name, a history, or a faith tradition to belong. Christians, Jews, Muslims, people of other faiths, and people of no faith can share a civic purpose while remaining different. The Constitution makes that possible; the moral labor of democracy makes it meaningful.
 A wave election signals political change, not proof of moral transformation. The revival begins after the votes are counted, when elected leaders decide whether to spend the trust they received on spectacle or service. If this Big Tent Revival is to endure, it must become more than a coalition that won. It must become a public witness that keeps faith with people across difference—and makes the common good something everyone can recognize in their daily lives.
 Rev. Dr. F. Willis Johnson is a spiritual entrepreneur, author, and scholar-practitioner whose leadership and strategies around social and racial justice issues are nationally recognized and applied.

 Love, Light and Courage
 Jessica A. Valencia 
 Nov 17, 2026 
 During my recent trip to Poland, I had the opportunity to meet Bernard Offen, a survivor of the Holocaust who became much more than just an interview subject to me.
 Prior to hearing Bernard’s story, I found myself in one of the darkest periods of my life. I felt worthless and hopeless, beginning to doubt whether basic human kindness was worth the energy when it seemed unreciprocated toward me or my community.
 Bernard experienced the horrific reality of the Holocaust, losing his father, mother, and sister. Throughout his storytelling, he focused on the importance of compassion, courage, and those who risked their lives to help others.
 Beyond sharing his personal experiences, Offen has dedicated his life’s work to encouraging younger generations to confront hatred, recognize the dangers of indifference, and understand their personal responsibility to protect human dignity. His message not only reassured me but also reshaped my perspective on daily life.
 I believe it is vital to educate ourselves and others during times of war and political division. In today’s climate, there is widespread hatred, confusion, and misinformation directed at people of various nationalities and beliefs.
 “If you don’t start looking at other people and make the heart [to heart] connection that we all have [to one another], whether you like it or not, that is the beginning of hatred for others and separation of others,” claimed Offen.
 Offen’s message about human connection extends beyond historical accounts of hatred. It serves as a reminder of how easily divisions can develop in modern societies, particularly when political rhetoric encourages people to view others as opponents rather than human beings.
 Whether through international conflicts or domestic political divisions, the consequences of dehumanization extend beyond borders. When people are reduced to political labels or viewed solely through the circumstances surrounding them, their individual experiences and humanity can be overlooked.
 “Imagine a blackboard and on that blackboard is written anti-jewish, second word anti-american, anti-black, anti-chinese, anti- and you go on and on through all the anti’s that you can place on there. When you erase the [root word] what you are left with is Anti, it is a position of ANTI- HUMAN.”
 Illustration: Jessica A. Valencia 
 The consequences of this mentality are not limited to international conflicts. They can also be seen in domestic policies and the rhetoric surrounding immigration, where entire communities can be targets of political division and public scrutiny. 
 This mindset is evident in the consequences of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act , enacted last July by President Donald J. Trump. The legislation increased the ICE budget, accelerated the removal of undocumented Americans, and spurred a pro-ICE sentiment across the country.
 This rhetoric has deepened the nation’s immigration divide, often obscuring the individual lives behind legal statuses. As a resident of Oxnard, a vibrant agricultural community of farmworkers, I see daily the importance of seeing the human beings involved in these debates. My neighbors and community members have their own stories, struggles, and families—none of which should be reduced to political stereotypes.
 A skyline overview of the agricultural beauty of Oxnard, Calif. (Credit: Jessica A. Valencia) 
 Trump has fueled pro-ICE sentiment by claiming that ‘Illegal immigration affects the lives of all Americans and causes burdens to American tax dollars, local schools, hospitals and communities by taking billions of dollars each year.’
 However, data from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) presents a different picture. Undocumented residents contribute nearly $97 billion in taxes despite being ineligible for many tax credits. Furthermore, many are unable to claim tax refunds due to concerns regarding their immigration status.
 Beyond tax contributions, undocumented residents play a crucial role in sustaining local economies. As ICE activity increases, fewer undocumented residents venture into public spaces, creating ripple effects that impact local schools, businesses, and workers.
 “One of our volunteers is one of the maintenance guys in the school district, he got his hours cut,” said Leonardo Martinez, a volunteer with VC Defensa , an organization created to support communities facing ICE activity in Ventura County. “He went weeks without work because the attendance of schools had tremendously decreased.”
 The decline in school attendance is just one example of how enforcement actions affect daily community life. Similar disruptions affect theaters, swap meets, and local or national Latine cultural centers and businesses, leading to lower revenues and forcing some to close.
 While these challenges continue to impact communities, education remains a vital tool for understanding history and recognizing acts of humanity during dark periods.
 That is the premise behind Bernard Offen’s educational initiative, “Love, Light and Courage,” which highlights acts of humanity and moral bravery during the Holocaust. His lifetime of activism—including his opposition to nuclear weapons—informs his perspective on what he describes as modern “evilzation.”
 “As a journalist you are [meant to] write civilization with a capital c but i write it with a very small c, because it is a very primitive and stupid civilization, and we are all part of it and what we do with it,” stated Offen. “I think we need to go back up in the trees for a thousand years before we call it a civilization, I call it an evilization [because, the world leaders do not care about us, to them we are just another number]”
 Bernard Offen shows off a tattoo reading “B-7815,” his identification number from Auschwitz-Birkenau. 
 In a world where political divisions, conflict, and misinformation shape how we perceive our neighbors, Offen’s message serves as a reminder that humanity should not be defined by nationality, religion, political affiliation, or immigration status. Recognizing humanity in others begins with a willingness to understand their experiences, regardless of how much they differ from our own.
 (Left) From left to right, Lilly Molina, Tadeo Cabrijo, Nicholas Hernandez, Bernard Offen, Jessica A. Valencia, Malory Shaw, and Ianis Soto meet and interview Offen. (Credit: Maria Morales, Fuente Latina) 
 Love, Light and Courage was first published by the Latino News Network and is republished with permission. 
 Jessica A. Valencia is a recent graduate from California State University. 
 Jessica was a fellow with Fuente Latina , an organization that sponsors journalists and students to visit Poland and learn about the Holocaust and Jewish history in the region.

 Care isn’t just comfort—it’s essential democratic labor. Discover why rebuilding trust, shared responsibility, and mutual care locally is vital for our future.
 Why Care Is the Foundation of Trust and Democracy
 Anatola Araba 
 Nov 12, 2026 
 What’s the first thing that comes to mind when you hear the word, “care”?
 For me, it was the Care Bears. Adorably colorful creatures that help soothe emotions when times are tough. In America’s cultural imagination, care is the equivalent of cuddling up with a fuzzy blanket or hugging a stuffed animal... or maybe I am just a hopeless Cancer sign who likes cozy things.
 It turns out this image is light years away from the reality of care.
 I’ve learned that care is hard, dirty work. Work that, despite being fundamental to democracy, is often offloaded to historically marginalized communities, women, and people of color. 
 I interviewed Joan Tronto, author of Caring Democracy , to gain a deeper understanding of what a caring society can look like. In her book, she defines care as “everything we do to maintain, continue, and repair our ‘world’ so that we can live in it as well as possible."
 But you can't create a culture of care without a foundation of trust.
 Growing up in New York City after the Twin Towers fell, I watched the Freedom Tower slowly rise downtown. Before it reached toward the sky, construction workers spent several years building its foundation. Architects know that if you want something to stand tall, the foundation must be strong.
 That is why, as members of the Democracy Architects council, we are on a mission to restore community, trust, and freedom in our democracy by 2030.
 In the book The Seven Rules of Trust , Wikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales argues, “the erosion of trust is a national emergency.”
 A Gallup poll shows only 32% of Americans trust the news media and only 16% trust the American government to do what’s right. Additionally, only 31% trust businesses to use AI responsibly. Yet trust is pivotal to progress. 
 So how do we rebuild trust? 
 The process has to happen locally. With the people who are closest to us. When people work toward a common interest they share and can act on, they build community and restore trust. 
 In Ancient Futures , author Helena Norberg-Hodge describes how, in traditional Ladakhi communities in the Himalayas, people once shared a strong sense of local responsibility. If a pipe broke in the community, people fixed it. Care for place was woven into daily life.
 But as Western-style development and more individualistic values entered the community, that shared responsibility began to erode. Broken pipes could sit in the street for months because people now waited for an outside system, like “the government,” to handle it. The issue was a shift in civic imagination: from “this is ours to care for” to “this is someone else’s job.”
 That connects directly to our cities now.
 As a member of the Youth250 bureau, I presented at a landmark event at the Declaration of Independence Center where Shania Bennett, who is currently running for Mayor of Philadelphia, made a similar point about local civic agency. 
 If you see trash on your block, she argued, that is also an invitation to notice your own relationship to the place you live. Who cares for this street? Who is responsible for this park? Who gets to feel ownership over the neighborhood's beauty and dignity?
 We need to value the work of care as essential democratic labor: the people who clean streets, pick up trash, repair pipes, maintain parks, and keep communities alive. They hold it all together. Because care is a skill. A practice. One that we too often disrespect. 
 One practical solution to this is to embed care into learning. 
 Children can be called upon to care for their classrooms, schools, and communities. In Children Framing Childhoods: Working-Class Kids' Visions of Care , Wendy Luttrell argues that students should see care as participation rather than punishment. Cleaning shared spaces, helping a classmate, tending a garden, or maintaining school materials, these all reinforce small civic practices. This does not replace the need for care workers. However, it helps shape the habits that inform how we treat our neighborhoods, cities, and public spaces. 
 Turns out the kindergarten classic says it best: “Clean up, clean up, everybody everywhere. Everybody do your share.” Honestly, that is democracy in a nutshell. Because democracy works best when everyone works together.
 It is hard to leave your trust in someone else’s hands, especially a stranger. However, rejecting the classic parental advice of “don’t talk to strangers”—especially strangers who are different from us—may be one of the things that can help our democracy most.
 In her book Talking to Strangers , Danielle Allen argues that putting strangers together for a common goal can lead to a more caring democracy. 
 A testament to this is Deliberative Polling, developed by Stanford professor James S. Fishkin. This method tests how people’s opinions can shift when they engage in conversation with people who think differently. Research showed that 70% of participants changed their minds on at least some individual key issues after deliberating together on issues that affect them. 
 I can attest to this personally. Growing up in New York City, not talking to strangers was a survival skill. But as I got older, talking to strangers has expanded my horizons in ways I never could have imagined. 
 It was a stranger’s encouragement that helped lead my art to a historic lunar museum, where it became the world’s first sci-fi short film on the Moon. Talking to strangers also led me to my first job out of college, writing for Elle and Harper’s Bazaar . Sometimes a stranger holds the key to a door that has been waiting for you to enter. 
 Culture gives us every reason for strangers not to have our best interests at heart. Yet we trust in those who make decisions with our wellbeing in mind. 
 The problem is not that we do not care, but rather that our care is directed at the wrong things. Journalism, politics, media, and technology often direct their care toward revenue, attention, and growth. Large corporations are perceived as profit-driven rather than focused on the well-being of society, causing public trust to plummet. 
 The digital landscape we live in often surrounds us with false care. 
 The Center for Humane Technology argues that algorithms do not care about our holistic well-being. They care about what keeps us scrolling. Young people are growing up in a time when a chatbot may be more available to talk about their emotions than the friends in their community. 
 Social media can make us feel connected to a community while leaving us alone in our rooms. The epidemic of loneliness we find ourselves in is fueled by not being called upon to care.
 The work now is to redirect care toward one another, our communities, and the shared world we are responsible for maintaining. To rebuild a culture of care, Joan Tronto argues, we must put care at the center of everything we do. 
 One way to practice care is service. I see service as an embodiment of agency. Doing something in your community, whether cleaning, organizing, volunteering, or showing up. Putting care into action is also how we find our people and our purpose. 
 Miraculous things can happen when we see people not as a means to an end, but as an end in themselves.
 In The Serviceberry , Robin Wall Kimmerer offers another way to think about the economics of care. She writes about reciprocity as an economic model for community life: not extraction, not endless transaction, but relationship. A healthy community is one where care circulates. 
 That matters because care is the paid and unpaid labor that keeps people alive: childcare, eldercare, cleaning, cooking, repairing, and maintaining the world around us. 
 This is where I want to emphasize the art of mutual care . 
 To me, mutual care means identifying what we already commonly care about across our differences, then using those shared concerns as a starting point to work toward collective goals. 
 When we focus on mutual care, issues can become less polarized. According to a Yale Program on Climate Change Communication study, while Democrats and Republicans had completely different reasons for caring about the environment, both sides shared a foundational priority: a safe and healthy environment for the next generation. 
 Rather than replacing our sense of community, technology can help us organize the foundation for real care to take place. Because real care requires gathering: organizing, cleaning, volunteering, and showing up together. And real care can be really hard work. 
 It turns out, care is not a perfectly wrapped care package with ribbons and sprinkle cookies.
 Care is a practice. A habit. Care is the essential work of maintaining, repairing, and continuing the world we share. 
 Care is also the foundation of trust and democracy. Democracy is about making decisions together, and trust is believing that other people can make decisions with our well-being in mind.
 That requires care. When people care, they are more likely to make decisions with our best interests at heart. And when we feel cared for, we are more able to trust.
 So if we want a culture of care, we have to teach people how to practice it: through media literacy, technology literacy, civic literacy, and real opportunities for local action.
 Because the question is not only, “What do you care about?”
 The question is: what do we mutually care about, and what are we willing to do about it together? 
 Anatola Araba is a futurist , filmmaker, and creative technologist whose work sits at the intersection of art, technology, and impact. She founded her studio, Reimagine Story Lab, and is a professor at New York University, where she teaches emerging media.

 Now It Is Time to Govern
 The Fulcrum 
 Nov 11, 2026 
 The votes have been cast. The campaigns have ended. The winners have celebrated, and the losers have begun to assess what comes next.
 For some Americans, the rancor or blame game will continue. But for many Americans, however, the most important question is neither who won nor who lost.
 It is whether anyone can govern. 
 Throughout this election season, candidates crisscrossed the country, promising solutions to the nation's challenges. Voters repeatedly identified the same concerns: affordability, health care, economic opportunity, immigration and border security, public safety, and the health of our democracy itself.
 Now comes the hard part.
 The campaign is over. The governing must begin.
 At The Fulcrum, we believe Americans deserve more than a return to continual campaigning. They deserve a serious examination of solutions that can attract support from conservatives, liberals, and independents alike.
 That is why today we are launching a new series: "Now It Is Time to Govern." 
 Over the coming months, we will explore practical, bipartisan , and evidence-based approaches to six issues that consistently rank among voters' highest priorities.
 This series will not ask how Democrats can defeat Republicans or how Republicans can defeat Democrats.
 Instead, it will ask a different question:
 What ideas have a realistic chance of improving people's lives while earning support across political divides? 
 Our goal is not false equivalency. Nor is it to pretend ideological differences don't matter. In a healthy democracy, disagreement is both unavoidable and necessary.
 But governing requires something more than disagreement. It demands negotiation, compromise, problem-solving, and a willingness to learn from what works.
 The challenges Americans face are too large and too pressing to remain permanent campaign talking points.
 When families struggle to pay for groceries, housing, and child care, affordability becomes more than a political slogan.
 When medical costs force families to choose between treatment and financial security, health care becomes more than a partisan issue.
 When workers worry about economic mobility, when communities face crime and addiction, when the nation wrestles with border security and immigration reform, and when citizens lose faith in democratic institutions, those problems cannot be solved through rhetoric alone.
 Solving our nation's problems requires leaders who respect all people, including groups that aren't vital to those leaders' reelection chances. It also requires leaders who stay open to new information and seek it out through research and analysis to broaden their horizons and effectively address the difficult problems facing our nation. Lastly, we need leaders willing to build bridges beyond their own constituency and encourage their supporters to do the same, with the goal of building the trust and understanding needed for competent governance. 
 And it requires a citizenry willing to demand more from elected officials than perpetual conflict.
 In each installment, The Fulcrum will examine reforms, proposals, and successful models from across the political spectrum. We will highlight ideas advanced by Republicans, Democrats, independents, academics, civic leaders, business leaders, and community organizations. Some proposals may be controversial. Others may already be quietly succeeding in states, cities, and communities across the country.
 The common denominator will be that they are serious attempts to address real problems.
 We believe a vast, often overlooked constituency remains in American life: citizens who care less about partisan victory than practical progress. They may disagree about policy details. They may vote differently. But they share a belief that governing should involve more than scoring political points.
 Too often, our political conversation rewards the loudest voices and the sharpest attacks. Yet history suggests many of America's greatest achievements came not from ideological purity, but from difficult cooperation among people who didn't agree on everything.
 Today's challenges demand the same spirit.
 Whether electoral mandates are narrow or decisive, the responsibility remains unchanged. Elections are not only about determining who holds power. They also create an opportunity, and an obligation, to use that power wisely. A decisive victory may give leaders more political capital, but it does not eliminate the need for effective governance, accountability, or public trust.
 This series will hold leaders accountable for that responsibility.
 We will ask what progress looks like. We will examine where cross-party cooperation is possible. We will spotlight innovative ideas that deserve broader attention. And we will challenge officials of both parties to explain not simply what they oppose, but what they propose. The election may have answered who will lead. It did not answer how we will solve our biggest challenges. That work begins now.
 The voters have rendered their verdict. The question before the nation is no longer who will lead, but whether those entrusted with power can deliver results.
 Now it is time to govern.
